newsitem.title: USA: U.S. presses ahead on Middle East summit.
newsitem.headline: U.S. presses ahead on Middle East summit.

text.p: The United States on Monday moved ahead with plans to hold a Middle East summit in Washington on Tuesday despite Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak's request for a postponement.
"If we're going to break the cycle of violence, we need a reengagement of the parties at the highest level, and a delay is not going to produce that," a White House official said.
The White House position was echoed by Dennis Ross, the U.S. coordinator for the Middle East peace talks.
"The president issued an invitation to Chairman Arafat. Chairman Arafat agreed to come. We expect him to be here," Ross said on NBC television's "Today" show.
Asked if the United States would agree to delay the talks because of Arafat's apparent reluctance to come, Ross replied: "We expect him to be here."
President Bill Clinton called the summit in an effort to end Israeli-Palestinian violence sparked by Israel's opening of a tunnel near Moslem shrines in Arab East Jerusalem.
Those invited to the summit include Arafat, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, King Hussein of Jordan and Mubarak. All but the Egyptian leader committed to attend.
The timing is critical not only because of last week's outbreak of bloody fighting in Gaza, the West Bank and Jerusalem, but also because of the U.S. presidential race.
Clinton is scheduled to hold the first of two campaign debates with Republican challenger Bob Dole in Hartford, Connecticut next Sunday, and planned to begin preparing for the encounter on Thursday.
